prompt: Is Captain Nair legal to cover pairing P-2201?

expected_answer.why: crew.json has 7 different crew members named *. Nair across 3 ranks and 2 bases (C-1042 A. Nair Captain/BLR, C-2295 S. Nair First Officer/BLR, C-3145 A. Nair Cabin Crew/BLR, C-3266 R. Nair Senior Cabin Crew/BLR, C-5020 K. Nair First Officer/DEL, C-5820 N. Nair Captain/BLR, C-5848 V. Nair Cabin Crew/BLR); 'Captain Nair' alone narrows this to exactly 2 (C-1042, C-5820), still ambiguous

explanation: A name is not an id in this dataset; the honest move is to list the (in this case 2) candidates and ask which one, or require the id.
historical_note: Empirically run against final_repo/backend (app.agent.entities.resolve): given 'Is Captain Nair legal to cover pairing P-2201?', the resolver returns crew_ids=['C-5837'] -- A. Sharma, who is not named Nair at all. It never matches on the name token; because P-2201 is mentioned and 'Captain' is recognised as a role, the _infer_missing() fallback in entities.py silently substitutes 'whoever holds the Captain seat on the pairing already named in the question', discarding the stated surname entirely. ents.unresolved and ents.ambiguous are both empty -- no signal reaches the answer that a name was involved at all. route() then proceeds at confidence 0.545 to LEGALITY_CHECK for C-5837. This is a fluent, confident, wrong substitution, not a refusal.
current_system_behaviour: FIXED (final_repo/backend, app/agent/entities.py). resolve() now scans a surname index built from world.crew before falling back to the pairing/role heuristic. Re-run: resolve('Is Captain Nair legal to cover pairing P-2201?', world) now returns crew_ids=[] and ents.ambiguous=[{'kind':'crew_name','candidates':['C-1042','C-5820'], ...}] -- the two real Captains named Nair -- instead of silently substituting C-5837 (A. Sharma). A surname that narrows to exactly one crew member (by surname plus stated rank) still resolves normally; a surname matching the wrong rank for everyone who holds it (e.g. 'Captain Bose', 0 of 7 Boses are Captains) reports unresolved rather than substituting. Covered by tests/test_routing_and_honesty.py's test_ambiguous_surname_is_flagged_not_silently_substituted, test_unique_surname_resolves_confidently and test_surname_with_no_matching_rank_is_unresolved_not_substituted.

prompt: Captain C-1042 calls in sick -- can First Officer C-1694 (his own First Officer on P-2291) legally cover the Captain's seat for the rest of the pairing?

expected_answer.why: a First Officer cannot legally act as the pairing's Captain; the seat requires Captain rank regardless of aircraft-type rating or duty-hour headroom

explanation: Rank-to-seat complement is a structural precondition enforced when rosters.json is authored (validate.py's own COMP table), but none of the seven rules in rules.json encode it -- RULE-QUAL-05 only checks aircraft *type*, not *rank*.
historical_note: Empirically run against final_repo/backend: `check_cover(world, 'C-1694', P-2291.days, exclude_pairing='P-2291')` -- i.e. exactly what the check_legality tool runs -- returns legal=True, issues=(). The rule engine (app/core/rules/engine.py) only evaluates RULE-QUAL-05/CERT-06/FDP-01/REST-04/DUTY-02/FLT-03; none of them check crew.rank against the seat being covered. The rank filter exists, but only inside candidates.py's enumerate_cover_for_pairing (which restricts its search to crew whose rank already matches the requested role) -- a direct check_legality(crew_id, pairing_id) or simulate_assignment call never passes through that filter, so it can return 'legal' for a candidate sitting in the wrong seat entirely.
current_system_behaviour: FIXED at the core layer (final_repo/backend, app/core/rules/precondition.py's new SeatRankRule, wired through CoverContext.required_role / check_cover's required_role= / check_legality's new role= parameter). Direct re-run: check_cover(world, 'C-1694', P-2291.days, exclude_pairing='P-2291', required_role='Captain') now returns legal=False, issues=("CONSTRAINT-RANK: C-1694 is a First Officer, not a Captain -- cannot legally hold the Captain's seat ...",). The natural-language layer (entities.py) also now captures this for the common single-crew-id phrasing -- 'Can First Officer C-1694 legally cover the Captain's seat on P-2291?' resolves seat_role='Captain' and LEGALITY_CHECK passes role='Captain' through -- but this question's original two-crew-id phrasing (naming both C-1042, who is sick, and C-1694, the candidate) still has a separate, smaller residual gap: entity resolution has no notion of 'which named crew_id is the subject of the question' when two are mentioned, and currently takes the first one (C-1042) as e.crew_id regardless of sentence role. That is a distinct problem from the one this question was written to probe (rank never being checked at all) and was left unfixed this pass; see docs/LIMITATIONS.md. Covered by tests/test_rules.py's test_wrong_rank_for_the_seat_is_illegal_when_a_seat_is_named and test_no_seat_named_keeps_every_prior_behaviour_unchanged (the default-None case, proving every one of the 38 shipped questions is bit-for-bit unaffected), and tests/test_routing_and_honesty.py's test_named_seat_differing_from_candidates_own_rank_is_captured.

expected_answer.why: rules.json defines exactly seven rules (RULE-FDP-01 .. RULE-BASE-07); there is no RULE-CREW-08

explanation: Grounding to the ruleset means saying a rule id doesn't exist, not guessing what a plausibly-named rule might mean.

prompt: C-3940 is showing a 0.71 disruption-risk score for tomorrow's pairing -- is keeping them on it a good idea?

expected_answer.why: this is the same policy judgement as 'should we pre-emptively swap C-1042 out given his 0.78 risk score' (already a documented decline case) -- risk_signals.json has no threshold that separates 'a good idea' from not

explanation: Rephrasing the canned policy example without its trigger words ('should we', 'pre-emptive', 'worth it') is exactly the kind of paraphrase a controller would actually type.
historical_note: Empirically run against final_repo/backend's router (app.agent.plans.route): this phrasing does NOT set policy_question=True. POLICY_RE requires one of a fixed list of trigger phrases ('should we/i ... pre-emptive|swap out|stand down|rest|replace|risk', 'is it worth', 'worth the/it', 'which is better', 'better overall', 'do you think/recommend we should', 'would you ... rather'); 'is keeping them on it a good idea?' matches none of them. The router instead scores this as RISK_LOOKUP (confidence 0.565) and would answer with the raw score and drivers -- not wrong on the facts, but it skips the honesty guard a controller relying on it would expect for a judgement call.
current_system_behaviour: PARTIALLY ADDRESSED (final_repo/backend, app/agent/plans.py's POLICY_RE). Widened from three literal trigger phrases to also match generic evaluative-judgement language ('good/bad/wise idea', 'makes sense to', 'is it advisable'). Re-run: this exact phrasing now sets policy_question=True and the router still reports intent=RISK_LOOKUP underneath it -- graph.py declines whenever policy_question is set regardless of which intent matched. This is still a pattern-matching fix, not a semantic one: a further paraphrase using none of the now-wider trigger words could still slip through the same way this one did. The architecturally complete fix -- routing evaluative-judgement detection through the LLM-classifier fallback plans.py's own docstring already describes as existing for 'genuinely novel questions', rather than growing POLICY_RE phrase by phrase -- was not implemented this pass.

Lowercase, no dashes, no punctuation -- the kind of input a controller actually types under pressure.

prompt: C-2087's licence is valid through 2026-09-18. Are they certified to operate on 2026-09-18 itself? What about the day after?
explanation: RULE-CERT-06 checks `valid_to < duty_date` as the failure condition (both the dataset generator and final_repo/backend's cert06.py agree) -- so the expiry date itself is the LAST legal day, not the first illegal one. Off-by-one here is exactly the 'fluent, confident and wrong' failure mode the problem statement warns about.

prompt: C-2143 has flown 79.28h in the 28 days ending 2026-09-20 (20.72h headroom under RULE-FLT-03). If they picked up an additional 21 flight-hours of duty, would RULE-FLT-03 be breached -- and would that stop them being offered as a legal cover candidate?
explanation: 79.28 + 21 = 100.28h, 0.28h over the 100h/28d limit -- arithmetically a breach. But whether that makes the candidate 'illegal' depends on which tool answers: it differs by design, see current_system_behaviour.
historical_note: Read directly from final_repo/backend/app/core/rules/flt03.py's own module docstring (titled 'KNOWN DATASET DISCREPANCY'): the original dataset generator (generate.py) lists RULE-FLT-03 in every option's rules_checked array but its check_cover() never actually evaluates it, so the shipped answer keys (scenarios.json/questions.json) never exercise a FLT-03 breach. To stay conformant with those answer keys, final_repo's flt03.py computes the real number but reports it at verdict='advisory' (STRICT=False by default), and models.py's RuleVerdict.is_breach / .passed treat 'advisory' as NOT a breach and AS passed -- so `check_cover`/`check_legality`/`enumerate_cover_candidates` will call this candidate legal regardless of the 21h add. `simulate_duty_window`, a separate code path with no engine/advisory concept, would instead report flight_breach=True for the same add-21h scenario. Two tools, same underlying arithmetic, two different verdicts on whether it's a breach -- because one was built to match the answer keys and the other wasn't. STRICT=True exists specifically to flip this and the module says the conformance harness runs both and reports when they disagree.
current_system_behaviour: FIXED (final_repo/backend, app/core/rules/flt03.py). The STRICT/advisory toggle was removed entirely -- RULE-FLT-03 now always reports 'breach' when over the limit, exactly like the other six rules, and RuleEngine no longer accepts a strict_flight_hours parameter. Re-running the full answer-key conformance suite (tests/conformance/test_answer_keys.py -- all 6 scenarios, 38 questions, 2 held-out scenarios) with this rule now hard-enforced: all still pass. The 'could exclude a candidate the shipped answer keys call legal' risk the old docstring warned about never actually materialised -- none of the shipped material comes anywhere near 100h/28d. `check_legality` / `enumerate_cover_candidates` / `simulate_duty_window` now agree on every FLT-03 question; the specific inconsistency this question demonstrated (two tools, one fact, two verdicts) no longer exists. Covered by tests/test_rules.py's test_flight_hour_breach_is_a_hard_gate_not_advisory and test_flight_hour_headroom_case_still_passes.

prompt: C-3305 has 56.4h of duty in the 7 days ending 2026-09-14 (3.6h headroom under RULE-DUTY-02). If they picked up exactly that much more duty, would they breach the limit? What about 0.1h more than that?
explanation: 60.0h exactly is legal -- the rule is 'max 60 duty hours', not 'fewer than 60'. Both the generator and final_repo's duty02.py use `total > max + EPS` (EPS=1e-6) as the breach test, so the boundary itself passes and 60.1h fails by exactly 0.1h.
